The **baritone** and the **euphonium** are the tenor-baritone voices of the brass family. Like every brass instrument, the sound starts with your
**lips buzzing** in a cup-shaped mouthpiece. This page follows a teacher's resource book (see the Works Cited); the words are this site's own.

Want to try the fingerings? The [Trumpet, Euphonium and Tuba fingering charts](brass-fingerings.qmd) have the baritone / euphonium chart in
**bass clef** and in **treble clef**, with a note explorer, a "which notes does this fingering play?" tool and a quiz.

## Where they came from {#history}

- The two instruments are **close relatives**. They have been called euphonium, baritone, baritone horn, tenor horn and tenor tuba, and the names
  have often been swapped, but the book says there is a real difference between the instrument called the baritone and the one called the euphonium.
- Both are pitched in **B♭** and were invented around the same time, in the **middle of the 1800s**, once valves (invented around **1815**) let makers
  build brass instruments for the tenor and baritone ranges.
- The book's one named date: in **1843** a German concertmaster, **Sommer of Weimar**, made a valved, bugle-style instrument with a baritone range,
  which came to be called a "Baryton". After that, many instruments appeared under the name "euphonium".
- Makers tried many designs: **as many as five valves**, a mix of **rotary and piston valves**, and different bell layouts. In the **late 1880s** in the
  United States the **double-bell euphonium** (one fixed bell and one you could point) appeared.
- Both are mainly **band instruments**, and both are often **solo** instruments.
- The book also covers the **E♭ alto horn** in this chapter because it is played the same way as the baritone.

## Baritone, euphonium, or alto horn? {#family}

| Instrument | What the book says |
|---|---|
| **Baritone** | B♭. Usually a **narrower bore** than the euphonium, so the tone is **light and clear**. The book groups it with the trumpet and trombone as a **cylindrical-bore** instrument. |
| **Euphonium** | B♭. A **conical bore**: the tube widens steadily along its whole length (like the cornet, flugelhorn, horn and tuba), so the tone is **softer and gentler**, "dark, rich and warm". Most have **four valves**. |
| **E♭ alto horn** | Similar to the baritone or tenor horn; played the same way. Its tuning notes are printed in treble clef (see below). |

*(These are the book's statements; the page has not checked them against another source.)*

## The parts {#parts}

The book labels a baritone and a euphonium (both shown with three valves; a euphonium often adds a fourth):

- **Mouthpiece**, **shank** (the narrow end that goes in), **mouthpiece receiver** and **lead pipe** (where the mouthpiece fits).
- **Bell**, and the **body** (the main tubing).
- **Valves 1, 2, 3**, each with its own **valve slide** (first, second, third), a **hook or ring** for the right thumb, the **main tuning slide** and the **water key**.

## Is it the right instrument for you? {#selecting}

The book lists three signs a student suits the baritone, euphonium or alto horn:

1. **Stature**: big enough to handle the instrument.
2. **Lips medium to thick**. (The book says thin lips suit trumpet and horn better.)
3. You can **sing a common folk song**.

## Putting it together and sitting {#posture}

**Assembly.** Put the mouthpiece in the receiver on the lead pipe and give it a **gentle twist**, not too tight.

**Posture and hands.**

1. Sit **up straight at the edge of the chair**, feet flat on the floor.
2. Hold the instrument up by the **vertical tubing with your left hand**.
3. Put your **right thumb in the hook or ring** near the valves.
4. Put the **tips of your first three fingers** on the valve buttons. The right hand makes a relaxed **"C"**, as if holding a tennis ball.
5. Keep your **wrists straight** and your **elbows away from your body**.

## Your embouchure and first sound {#embouchure}

1. **Wet your lips** and shape your mouth and throat as if you were saying **"oh"**. Bring the lips together as if saying **"em"**.
2. Take a **full breath through the mouth** and blow through the closed lips. You are making a **relaxed buzz**.
3. Take the mouthpiece off the instrument and hold it by the **shank**. Set it **over the middle of the buzz**, **half on the upper lip and half on the lower**, without pressing hard. **Check in a mirror.**
4. Breathe in fully and play a **long, steady buzz** on the mouthpiece.

The book's checklist for any brass player: sitting straight, head up, left hand and wrist, right hand and wrist, instrument held right for your body,
fingers gently curved, elbows away, mouthpiece in the right place, **lip corners firm and the centre relaxed**, chin flat and pointed, breathing well, relaxed buzz.

## When the tone goes wrong {#tone-problems}

| What you hear | Possible causes | Try this |
|---|---|---|
| 1. No tone, rushing air | embouchure not firm enough; blowing, not buzzing; air stream squeezed (closed throat, high tongue) | firm up the embouchure; buzz the lips without the mouthpiece; say "oh" to open the throat and keep the tongue down |
| 2. Thin, pinched tone | embouchure too tight, lips pinched; too little air between the lips | relax the embouchure; breathe fully and use faster air |
| 3. Garbled tone | embouchure not firm enough; lips folding over the teeth | firm it up; re-form it and use the mouthpiece ring to check where the lips are |
| 4. Stopped or intense air | lips pinched shut; too little air between the lips | relax the embouchure; check the tongue with "oh" and use faster air |
| 5. Sharp in the upper register | too much pressure on the embouchure | faster air, less pressure |
| 6. Flat, flabby low notes | slow air; floppy embouchure | faster air; firm up the embouchure |
| 7. Hard to play high | not enough air speed | increase the air speed |
| 8. Hard to play low | air too fast; too much pressure | slow the air; relax the embouchure |

## Tuning {#tuning}

- A good **tone** matters most: "you can't tune a poor tone".
- Play and **slur up to one of the book's tuning notes** so the embouchure stays natural. The book prints them as **written F3 for beginners and B♭3 for more advanced players**
  on the bass-clef baritone / euphonium (both are the open, no-valve notes). In treble clef the written notes are **G4** and **C5**.
- If the pitch is **sharp**, **pull the main tuning slide out**; if **flat**, **push it in**.
- Then tune each **valve slide** on a note that uses that valve. A small change of the main slide should not need new valve-slide settings.
- The book also draws the notes that tend to be **sharp** and **flat** on the instrument; this page does not copy them.

## Fingering charts {#charts}

The book's baritone / euphonium chart is a table of notes with the valves to press. A few things it shows:

- Bass clef is **concert pitch**: the open (no valves) notes are **B♭2, F3, B♭3, D4, F4, B♭4**.
- The **treble-clef** chart is the same fingerings, written a **major ninth** higher than they sound (written F♯3 on 1-2-3 sounds E2). The Brass page lets you flip between concert and written pitch.
- **Four valves.** The book prints a second fingering for instruments with four valves: **4** instead of **1-3**, and **2-4** instead of **1-2-3**.
  Open this on the [fingering charts](brass-fingerings.qmd#explore).
- The book does not give separate fingerings for a **compensating** euphonium.

## Daily care {#care}

**Putting it away.**

1. Press the **water key** and **blow** (not buzz) to empty the water. Empty each **valve slide** too.
2. **Wipe the instrument** with a soft clean cloth.
3. **Push all the slides in**, pressing the matching valve each time you move one.
4. Take out the mouthpiece and put both in the case. **Latch** the case.

**Oiling the valves (daily).**

1. **Unscrew only the first valve** at the top of the valve casing (not the button). Do not turn the valve or touch the part the casing protects.
2. Put **5 or 6 drops** of valve oil along the metal part with the holes.
3. Slip it back in. On the euphonium or baritone **line up the valve guide with its groove in the casing**. (On the alto horn, turn the button **clockwise** until it clicks.) Screw the valve in at the top.
4. **Push the button up and down quickly** to work in the oil.
5. Do the **other valves** the same way.

**Greasing the slides (regularly).** One slide at a time: press the matching valve and pull the slide out (the main tuning slide needs no valve);
wipe off the old grease; put on a **generous** layer of new grease; put the slide back **with the valve pressed**; move it in and out to spread the grease;
push it in and wipe off the extra; leave it where it was. Repeat with the other slides.
